threatModel.deployment: One club operates one Courtside instance behind the reference proxy with PostgreSQL and server-side sessions.

surfaces.description: Public HTML shell, court plan, static assets and PWA lifecycle.
Login, bootstrap, initial password and brute-force controls.
Server-side sessions, CSRF, logout, expiry and credential changes.
Bookings, series, participants and personal booking data.
Facility, cards, rules and club configuration administration.
People, accounts, roles, memberships and membership types.
CSV snapshots, previews, external references and full synchronization.
Contract-first JSON boundary and RFC 9457 error surface.
Caddy, container runtime, network and PostgreSQL topology.
Candidate image, dependencies, SBOM, provenance and signature.
Logs, metrics, backups, restores and retained evidence.

trustBoundaries.description: Untrusted browser and network traffic enters through Caddy.
Forwarded identity and transport metadata crosses into Spring Boot.
Application data and server-side sessions enter PostgreSQL.
Source and dependencies become a signed container image.
Operational commands create logs, backups and security evidence.

safe.description: Bounded passive and non-destructive checks that do not alter domain state or exhaust resources.

active.description: Curated authentication, authorization, mutation and injection attacks against a disposable target.

destructive.description: Bounded exhaustion and protocol-abuse checks that may make the disposable target unavailable.

passed.description: Every selected control executed with complete evidence and no unaccepted validated finding.

incomplete.description: A tool, prerequisite, target proof, control or required evidence is missing or failed to execute.

failed.description: A secure outcome was violated or a validated finding remains outside an unexpired acceptance.

severity.releasePolicy: Blocks release until fixed and retested.
Blocks release unless an explicit unexpired acceptance records compensating controls.
Requires an owned remediation or time-bounded acceptance.
Recorded and prioritized with product context.

controls.rationale: The control asks for parameterized operating-system calls or contextual command-line encoding. The shipped application starts no operating-system process at all: it constructs no ProcessBuilder and calls no Runtime.getRuntime, so no request value ever reaches a command line. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoInterpreterIsThereForAnInjectionToReach goes red the moment one appears in src/main/java.

The control asks for protection against LDAP injection. The shipped application binds to no directory: it carries no JNDI directory context, no LdapContext and no LDAP client, and accounts live in its own PostgreSQL schema. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoInterpreterIsThereForAnInjectionToReach goes red the moment one appears in src/main/java.

The control asks for query parameterization or precompiled queries against XPath injection. The shipped application evaluates no XPath: it constructs no XPathFactory and reads no XML document at all. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoInterpreterIsThereForAnInjectionToReach goes red the moment one appears in src/main/java.

The control asks that a LaTeX processor is configured without --shell-escape and behind a command allowlist. Courtside runs no LaTeX processor and generates no typeset documents; its exports are CSV written by commons-csv. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoInterpreterIsThereForAnInjectionToReach goes red the moment one appears in src/main/java.

The control asks that special characters in regular expressions are escaped so they are not misread as metacharacters. Every Pattern.compile in src/main/java takes a string literal written in this repository, so no request value ever decides what a metacharacter means. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingEveryCompiledPattern_thenItsSourceIsALiteralAndNotARequest goes red for a pattern built from anything else.

The control asks that untrusted HTML from a WYSIWYG editor or similar is sanitized by a known library. Courtside accepts no HTML from anybody: it ships no rich-text editor, carries no HTML sanitizer dependency, and its frontend renders every club-entered value as React text, using neither dangerouslySetInnerHTML nor innerHTML anywhere in frontend/src.

The control asks that eval and other dynamic code execution such as Spring Expression Language are avoided. The shipped application evaluates no expression language: it carries no SpelExpressionParser, no javax.script engine and no scripting shell, and its rule engine evaluates declarative rows rather than expressions. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoInterpreterIsThereForAnInjectionToReach goes red the moment one appears in src/main/java.

The control asks that user-supplied scriptable or expression template content such as Markdown, CSS or XSL stylesheets is sanitized or disabled. Courtside accepts none: it renders no Markdown and carries no Markdown, BBCode or XSL dependency, and the only club-entered value that reaches a stylesheet is the club colour, which the API document constrains to a hex literal and HexColorPatternTest keeps constrained in all three of its copies.

The control asks that templates are not built from untrusted input. Courtside builds none: its message templates come from the shipped i18n bundles, MailTemplates substitutes named placeholders into that fixed text rather than compiling anything a request supplied, and there is no server-side template engine on the classpath at all.

The control asks that untrusted input is sanitized before use in JNDI queries and that JNDI is configured safely. The shipped application performs no JNDI lookup: it carries no InitialContext and no javax.naming use, and its only datasource is configured by Spring Boot properties. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoInterpreterIsThereForAnInjectionToReach goes red the moment one appears in src/main/java.

The control asks that content is sanitized before it is sent to memcache. Courtside runs no memcache: it carries no memcached client, and the only caches it keeps are in-process maps holding hash-prefix ranges. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoInterpreterIsThereForAnInjectionToReach goes red the moment one appears in src/main/java.

The control asks that format strings which could resolve unexpectedly are sanitized before processing. No format string in Courtside comes from a request: every log statement uses the parameterized {} form this repository requires, and the String.format calls in src/main/java take literals written here with the request value as an argument rather than as the pattern.

Courtside's shipped application code is Java and TypeScript running in managed-memory runtimes. It contains no native string-copy, pointer-arithmetic or manually allocated memory path to which this control's memory-safe function requirements apply.

The control asks that XML parsers are configured restrictively so external entities cannot be resolved. The shipped application parses no XML: it constructs no DocumentBuilder, SAXParser, XMLInputFactory, TransformerFactory or XmlMapper, and its request and response bodies are JSON generated from the OpenAPI document. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoInterpreterIsThereForAnInjectionToReach goes red the moment one appears in src/main/java.

Courtside validates public request structures through its OpenAPI contract and records selected domain invariants in code and design documentation, but does not maintain a closed inventory of every validation rule. Completing such an inventory would document existing behavior rather than change the shipped product, so this control remains blocked without creating remediation work.

Courtside enforces cross-field invariants at request and domain boundaries, but does not maintain a closed document mapping every related-field consistency rule to every production workflow. Producing that map would document existing behavior rather than change the shipped product, so this control remains blocked without creating remediation work.

Courtside enforces selected per-account and global business limits through booking rules and bounded workflows, but does not maintain a closed inventory of every such limit. Completing that inventory would document existing behavior rather than change the shipped product, so this control remains blocked without creating remediation work.

controls.rationale: Courtside does not rely on a CORS preflight to protect sensitive operations. Spring Security requires a matching CSRF cookie and request header on browser writes, including requests whose media type or method would not cause a preflight.

The control asks that separate applications sit on different hostnames so the same-origin policy and host-scoped cookies separate them. Courtside is one application on one hostname per club: the reference deployment serves the single-page application, its assets and the API from that one origin, and there is no second application on it to be separated from.

The control asks that messages received over postMessage are discarded when the origin is untrusted or the syntax is invalid. Courtside registers no message listener in frontend/src, so no such message reaches application code. The service worker vite-plugin-pwa generates accepts only the browser's own client messages, which the browser already restricts to this instance's origin.

controls.rationale: The control asks that an automatic redirect to a hostname the application does not control happens only to an allowlisted destination. Courtside redirects to no other hostname: its only application-initiated navigation is the fixed same-origin path /login, and its server issues no redirect built from a request value.

The control asks for a query allowlist, depth limiting, amount limiting or cost analysis against expensive nested GraphQL queries. Courtside serves no GraphQL and no other client-composed query language; every operation is a fixed REST route declared in the OpenAPI document.
The control asks that GraphQL introspection is disabled in production. Courtside ships no GraphQL schema and no introspection endpoint to disable.

The control asks that WebSocket connections use WSS. Courtside opens no WebSocket: neither src/main/java nor frontend/src constructs one, and the browser talks to the instance over HTTPS requests only.

The control asks that the Origin header is checked against an allowlist during the WebSocket handshake. Courtside performs no WebSocket handshake, so there is no upgrade request whose origin could be trusted.

The control asks that a dedicated WebSocket token meets the session-management requirements where standard session management cannot be used. Courtside has no WebSocket channel and therefore issues no token beside its ordinary session cookie.

The control asks that a dedicated WebSocket token is obtained through the already authenticated HTTPS session when a session transitions to a WebSocket channel. No session in Courtside ever makes that transition, because no WebSocket channel exists.

The control asks that a compressed file is checked against a maximum uncompressed size and file count before it is expanded. Courtside expands nothing: a roster snapshot is uploaded as delimited text with a declared encoding and separator, and the shipped application constructs no archive or decompression stream at all. InterpreterSurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoInterpreterIsThereForAnInjectionToReach goes red the moment one appears in src/main/java.

The control asks that file paths for file operations are built from internally generated or trusted data rather than from a submitted filename. Courtside builds no path from an upload: a club logo and a roster snapshot are read as in-memory bytes, the logo is stored as a column beside its canonical media type and digest, and every name a download carries is built by ExportAdminController from the export kind and the date, never from anything a club typed.

The control asks that a user's identity cannot be spoofed through a second identity provider sharing a user identifier. Courtside integrates no identity provider at all, so no external namespace ever names one of its accounts. AuthenticationPathwaySurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoIdentityProviderIntegrationIsThere goes red if an integration appears.

Courtside consumes no authentication assertion: a member proves who they are with a password this instance stores the hash of. The control asks that every system creating and managing sessions in a federated identity ecosystem is documented together with the controls coordinating their lifetimes. Courtside participates in no federation: it creates every session itself, ends every session itself, and integrates no single sign-on system.

controls.rationale: This control asks a multi-tenant application for cross-tenant controls. Courtside is single-tenant by design: one club, one instance, one database, with no tenant discriminator on any row and no operation that can name another tenant. There is no second tenant for an operation to affect.

The control asks that a self-contained token is validated by its signature or MAC before its contents are trusted. Courtside issues no self-contained token: its sessions are Spring Session JDBC rows in the instance's own PostgreSQL database, and the cookie carries an opaque identifier that names a row rather than any content to tamper with.

The control asks for an algorithm allowlist that excludes 'None' when creating and verifying self-contained tokens. Courtside creates no such token and verifies none, so no algorithm field reaches any decision it makes.

The control asks that key material validating self-contained tokens comes from pre-configured trusted sources rather than from headers such as jku, x5u or jwk. Courtside validates no token and reads no JWS header; a session identifier is looked up in its own database.
The control asks that a token's nbf and exp validity span is verified. Courtside's session validity is a column on the stored session row that the server owns, not a claim the client presents.

The control asks that a service checks a token's type and intended purpose before accepting its contents. Courtside accepts one credential shape, an opaque session identifier resolved against its own session store, so there is no second token type it could confuse with the first.

The control asks that a service only accepts tokens whose audience names it. A Courtside session row exists only in the instance that created it and is unusable anywhere else, so there is no audience claim to restrict.

The control asks that an issuer signing for several audiences restricts each token to its intended audience. Courtside issues no signed token and serves one club per instance, so no token can be presented to an audience it was not made for.

The control asks that tokens reach only the components that need them, such as keeping access and refresh tokens in a backend-for-frontend rather than in the browser. Courtside implements no OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect role: it is no client, resource server, authorization server or OpenID Provider, registers no client, issues and accepts no access, refresh or ID token, and signs a member in with a form-posted password against its own account table. AuthenticationPathwaySurfaceTest#whenReadingTheShippedSource_thenNoIdentityProviderIntegrationIsThere goes red if an integration appears.

tests.title: Authentication and brute-force boundaries
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Invalid and abusive authentication attempts cannot enumerate or take over an account and remain rate limited across path variants.

tests.title: Administrative multi-factor authentication
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Administrative access requires the documented ASVS Level 2 authentication strength.
tests.rationale: Courtside does not yet provide a second factor for administrators.

tests.title: Session lifecycle and browser isolation
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Login rotates the session and logout, expiry, password change and authority removal invalidate stale access without browser-history disclosure.

tests.title: Operation, role and object authorization matrix
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Every operation and object is accessible only to explicitly authorized roles and owners, with rejected attempts leaving state unchanged.

tests.title: Booking integrity under competing and abusive requests
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Competing writes preserve one occupancy, authorization, participant capacity and idempotency without partial state.

tests.title: Participation consent and personal-data isolation
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: A participant can discover and withdraw only their own participation without resolving another person's identity.

tests.title: Configuration administration boundaries
prerequisites: Existing facility, card and rule resources
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Only authorized fields and operations can change club configuration, with conflicts and invalid references leaving state unchanged.

tests.title: People, account and membership administration
prerequisites: Synthetic roster with ownership and role boundaries
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Person, account, role and membership mutations cannot cross role or person boundaries or expose unrelated personal fields.

tests.title: Snapshot parser and synchronization abuse
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Malformed, oversized, ambiguous and conflicting snapshots cannot escape parsing limits, take over accounts or leave a partial synchronization.

tests.title: Browser injection and client-side data retention
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Untrusted values remain data, CSP violations are observable and personal data is unavailable from browser storage after session termination.

tests.title: Proxy, TLS and runtime exposure
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: The proxy and runtime expose only intended routes and methods, preserve trusted forwarding boundaries and use the documented TLS and container controls.

tests.title: Source, dependency and candidate-image evidence
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Required static and dependency evidence is complete, exceptions are current and release attestations bind to the assessed digest.

tests.title: Contract-bound malformed input and error handling
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Malformed and boundary inputs produce stable typed failures without undocumented routes, unhandled exceptions or partial state.

tests.title: Adversarial resource consumption and recovery
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Bounded attacker-shaped load stops before host limits, preserves integrity and leaves the service recoverable.

tests.title: Sensitive operational data and recovery evidence
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Logs, metrics, backups and assessment evidence contain no credentials or unintended personal data and retain sufficient provenance for recovery and investigation.

tests.title: Bounded authenticated dynamic application scan
prerequisites: Pinned ZAP image and rule policy
tests.expectedSecureOutcome: Authenticated discovery and curated active rules remain inside the approved read-only routes, retain every scanner alert as an untriaged candidate and fail closed on lost authentication or coverage.
